results.title: Ghana risks losing a generation to drug abuse – Afenyo-Markin
results.content: Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin has warned that Ghana risks losing a generation of young people to drug abuse, calling for urgent action to address the effects of narcotics trafficking on communities. He said the proliferation of illicit drugs threatens the health and future of young people, destroys families and undermines national productivity. Speaking at a press briefing ahead of Parliament's resumption on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, he said the consequences of drug trafficking extended beyond national security and Ghana's international reputation. “The proliferation of illicit drugs threatens the health and the future of our young people. It destroys families, undermines productivity, and places an increasing burden on our healthcare and social welfare systems. We risk losing a generation of young people whose potential should be contributing to the development of our country

results.title: Minority files motion to review Bagbin’s ruling on proposed drug trafficking probe
results.content: The Minority in Parliament has filed a motion seeking a review of Speaker Alban Bagbin's ruling that declared inadmissible its proposed parliamentary inquiry into drug trafficking through Ghana. On September 29, 2026, Speaker Alban Bagbin ruled the Minority's proposed inquiry inadmissible, citing the risk that it could prejudice ongoing criminal proceedings involving approximately 21 persons in four separate narcotics-related cases. The ruling followed the Minority's attempt to secure a bipartisan parliamentary inquiry into major narcotics seizures linked to Ghana. The motion, filed by First Deputy Minority Whip and Tolon MP Habib Iddrisu, invokes Standing Order 127 of Parliament's Standing Orders.

results.title: Vehicles do not commit crimes: Registered-Owner liability, the presumption of innocence, and the legality of TRAFFITECH-GH
results.content: The legitimacy of an enforcement system depends not only on the soundness of its objectives but on the lawfulness of its methods. TRAFFITECH-GH pursues a vital public purpose, yet in its present form it substitutes a register of title for proof of conduct and asks the citizen to prove his own innocence. Ghanaian criminal law knows no general doctrine of vicarious liability that would justify the former, and the Constitution and the Evidence Act forbid the latter absent clear legislative warrant. Until Parliament supplies that warrant, a registered owner who receives a notice for an offence he did not commit is entitled to require the prosecution to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, that he was the driver. Vehicles do not commit crimes. Persons do, and the law must identify the right person before it punishes anyone.
